The current study examined the effect of cell phone use on the percentage of cones hit in different weather conditions (dry, wet, and icy). After informed consent, participants were randomized to a cell phone group: no cell (n = 15) and cell (n = 15). After randomization, they completed a 10-minute driving course on a driving simulator programmed to dry, wet, and icy conditions. Participants completed the course 3 times, once in each of the three weather conditions. Participants needed to keep their vehicle within 2 rows of meandering cones, and the percentage of cones hit during each course was measured. We hypothesized that the size of the difference between the cell phone groups would vary depending on the weather condition.

This article uses a meta-analysis to try and understand the effects of a flipped classroom on students' learning achievement and motivation, as well as what moderator variables influence these effects. The authors found that flipped classrooms do have an overall positive effect on students’ achievement and motivation. As for moderating variables, the research showed that the type of pre-class media had a big impact on the effectiveness of the flipped classroom, with videos being the most successful. It also showed variations in studies across regions, with developing nations having the biggest difference from traditional models. Most importantly for our research, the study showed that there are differences between the effects of flipped classrooms in different subjects. Their research showed more positive impacts for flipped classrooms in the natural sciences and other STEM fields than in the social sciences. This indicates that there is a difference worth studying; however, a meta-analysis is not the same as a study focused on just that variable, and so our research would still be valuable.

This study asks whether flipped classrooms actually improve student achievement in STEM courses compared to traditional teaching. Using a meta-analysis of 53 previous studies, the authors found that flipped learning has a positive effect on student performance, which means students in flipped classrooms generally do better than those in traditional settings. The most successful flipped models included structured pre-class work and in-class group activities. For our research, this article is important because it provides evidence that flipped classrooms can actually improve learning outcomes. Even though it focuses on only STEM, it supports our larger question about whether flipped classrooms can meaningfully improve student experience and learning across all disciplines, including the humanities.

Sitting in the University Chapel listening to Dr. U’s lecture, I first wondered how I could apply a chemistry lecture using social psychological concepts. But, looking deeper than the chemical technicalities, which I remember mostly none of them, the things I remembered the most were the social aspects of the lecture. Firstly, the overarching lesson to question the form of any painting you’re presented reminds me of how we easily accept societal rules. In this case, we expect things in museums to be in their preserved original form; we have this assumption that they are all exactly as the author first intended. Questioning the form you are presented with and seeking deeper truths is a form of going against social norms to accept what you see in a museum. Also, Dr. U giving acknowledgements for about 10 minutes at the start of the lecture made him seem extremely approachable and down to earth. It stems from how we perceive people’s actions as a reflection of their internal selves. We tend to dislike a narcissistic person and prefer one who is more engaging, bubbly, and grateful. So, our actions matter in getting people to engage with us and our work.

The proposed replacement of the Buy Low grocery store on James Jackson Parkway with a self-storage facility is far more than a zoning dispute, it is a matter of food access and community well-being. For many residents in West Atlanta, Buy Low is the only full-service grocery store within walking distance and serves as a critical resource for families, seniors, and individuals without reliable transportation. The only other nearby option, the Grocery Spot, operates as a free food pantry that provides essential assistance to households experiencing food insecurity. While the Grocery Spot plays a vital role in addressing hunger, it is not a replacement for a grocery store where residents can regularly purchase fresh food, household necessities, and other everyday items. Losing Buy Low would leave the community with virtually no place to shop for groceries locally, forcing many residents to travel several miles for basic necessities. This is an impossible task for those without access to a car or dependable public transportation.

As mentioned above, we dwelt a lot on how to analyze data in a reproducible and ethically responsible manner. While working on code in our R script/RMarkdown, Dr. Johnson advised us to put a reason behind each of our analytical decisions; this is so that other analysts reading our code can understand why we made certain decisions that resulted in certain conclusions. Even when deciding whether to keep or remove an outlier, we need to explain our reasoning so that our analysis can be reproduced. We didn’t focus much on collecting data in this course at all, except the essential topics of informed consent and confidentiality.

When dealing with conflict, I used to shrink away from it because I’d always seen disagreement as a relationship breaker. As Amy Gallo said, I thought disagreeing with someone would make them like you less or think you don’t like them, so, in an effort to be nice, I would avoid disagreement or conflict because it seemed like the easiest route. But for a while now, after attending various workshops on managing conflict and disagreement, I’ve learned and worked on things that echo the TED Talk on how to approach disagreements with others. Moving forward, setting goals when I find myself in a conflict with others will help me not take it personally. One thing I learned from the article is that it’s also important to see conflict as an opportunity to fix something within ourselves. One question I have is how we can move past conflicts when the other side refuses to meet us at our level. Sometimes you can self-reflect on your end, but the other party remains stubborn. Regardless, I now understand more that silence solves nothing; instead, it can hurt more than disagreement does. Just as we learned from Hicks on dignity, staying silent in the face of conflict can make the other party believe you don’t care about their point of view, violating their dignity.

Karen’s mothering also extends to Gene when her anxieties about him raise because she doesn’t believe what he says. Karen has no prior knowledge of Gene’s past, except for his drinking habits. Chaon writes: “She didn’t know what a bad person he’d been” (7). Her knowledge of Gene’s past was limited, so she didn’t worry all that much about him. She chose to believe in what she wanted to believe in. She once told Gene early in their marriage” I never believed that anything terrible could happen to me”, and when Gene cautioned her against saying that she said his superstitiousness was cute (Chaon 16). Chaon’s inclusion of this flashback has an element of foreshadowing, especially once this statement is recalled as Karen dies in the fire. Karen’s dismissal of Gene’s past went against her mothering tendencies to know everything and receive assurance from whatever source she could. When she starts to lack trust in Gene’s words, she begins to mother him. The night of the fire, she gives him a kind of motherly timeout. She says, “I don’t want to talk to you until you’re ready to tell me the truth” (Chaon 25). After a whole marriage of not knowing the details of Gene’s past, at the slightest inclination that there’s something Gene could be hiding from her in the present, she raises her defenses. She doesn’t know how to react, so she resorts to her mothering tendencies. She doesn’t believe Gene when he says he is no longer drinking. Karen’s defenses when she doesn’t understand a situation is to mother the situation, elevating the situation beyond proportion.
